title: When do you use OkHttp `MockWebServer` (a real local HTTP server to test outbound `WebClient`/`RestClient` calls — verify request method/path/headers, simulate 404/500/timeout/retry) versus `WebTestClient` (in-memory, for testing your own reactive controllers with `@WebFluxTest` + `@MockBean`)?
shortTitle: When to use OkHttp MockWebServer versus WebTestClient — testing outbound HTTP calls versus testing your own reactive controllers

s1_definition.profdef: OkHttp `MockWebServer` and Spring's `WebTestClient` solve opposite testing problems. `MockWebServer` is a real, lightweight HTTP server that starts on a local port and lets you script responses, so you point your application's outbound client — a `WebClient` or `RestClient` calling a downstream service — at it and assert the exact request your code sent, while simulating downstream behavior like 404, 500, slow responses, and retries. `WebTestClient` is an in-memory test client for your own inbound endpoints, used with `@WebFluxTest` and mocked collaborators, to verify that your reactive controllers handle requests, validation, status codes, and response bodies correctly. In short, `MockWebServer` tests the calls your service makes outward to others, and `WebTestClient` tests the calls others make inward to your service.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India's payments service as a bank teller. There are two very different things you want to test about this teller. First, when the teller has to phone an outside credit bureau to check a score, does the teller dial the right number, say the right things, and handle it correctly if the bureau is busy, gives a wrong-number error, or does not pick up? To test that, you set up a fake phone line that pretends to be the bureau and listens to exactly what the teller says — that fake phone line is MockWebServer, testing the teller's OUTGOING calls. Second, when a customer walks up to the teller's counter and hands over a transfer form, does the teller validate it, reject bad forms with the right message, and process good ones correctly? To test that, you play the role of the customer walking up to the counter — that is WebTestClient, testing the INCOMING requests your own teller handles.
s1_definition.oneliner: MockWebServer tests the outbound calls your service makes to downstream services; WebTestClient tests the inbound requests your own controllers receive.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OkHttp `MockWebServer` and Spring's `WebTestClient` solve opposite testing problems. `MockWebServer` is a real, lightweight HTTP server that starts on a local port and lets you script responses, so you point your application's outbound client — a `WebClient` or `RestClient` calling a downstream service — at it and assert the exact request your code sent, while simulating downstream behavior like 404, 500, slow responses, and retries. `WebTestClient` is an in-memory test client for your own inbound endpoints, used with `@WebFluxTest` and mocked collaborators, to verify that your reactive controllers handle requests, validation, status codes, and response bodies correctly. In short, `MockWebServer` tests the calls your service makes outward to others, and `WebTestClient` tests the calls others make inward to your service.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India's payments service as a bank teller. There are two very different things you want to test about this teller. First, when the teller has to phone an outside credit bureau to check a score, does the teller dial the right number, say the right things, and handle it correctly if the bureau is busy, gives a wrong-number error, or does not pick up? To test that, you set up a fake phone line that pretends to be the bureau and listens to exactly what the teller says — that fake phone line is MockWebServer, testing the teller's OUTGOING calls. Second, when a customer walks up to the teller's counter and hands over a transfer form, does the teller validate it, reject bad forms with the right message, and process good ones correctly? To test that, you play the role of the customer walking up to the counter — that is WebTestClient, testing the INCOMING requests your own teller handles.

**One line to remember:** MockWebServer tests the outbound calls your service makes to downstream services; WebTestClient tests the inbound requests your own controllers receive.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the direction of the call, because that is the whole decision. If the thing under test is code that calls out to another service — a `WebClient` or `RestClient` fetching a credit score, posting to a payment gateway, or reading an exchange rate — then the collaborator you need to fake is the downstream server. `MockWebServer` is exactly that: a genuine HTTP server from the OkHttp project that binds to an ephemeral local port. You enqueue scripted `MockResponse` objects, point your client at the server's URL, run your code, and then two things happen. Your client really sends a real HTTP request over the loopback interface, and the server records it as a `RecordedRequest` you can inspect. This lets you assert the method, path, query string, headers, and body that your code produced, which matters because bugs often live in how you build the outbound request — a wrong header, a missing query parameter, a malformed path.

`MockWebServer` shines at simulating downstream failure, which is the hard part of resilient client code. You enqueue a `MockResponse` with status 500 to verify your retry logic retries, a 404 to verify you map it to the right domain exception, and `setBodyDelay` or `setHeadersDelay` to simulate a slow server so you can verify your client's timeout fires. Because it is a real server speaking real HTTP, it exercises the full client stack — connection, serialization, status handling — not a mock of the client. In code: `server.enqueue(new MockResponse().setResponseCode(500)); String baseUrl = server.url("/").toString(); CreditScoreClient client = new CreditScoreClient(WebClient.create(baseUrl)); assertThrows(DownstreamException.class, () -> client.fetchScore("SAV2001")); RecordedRequest req = server.takeRequest(); assertEquals("/scores/SAV2001", req.getPath());`.

Now the other direction. If the thing under test is your own controller — the code that receives requests — then you do not need a fake downstream; you need a client that drives your endpoints. `WebTestClient` is that client, and with `@WebFluxTest` Spring loads only the web layer, not the whole application, so the test is fast and focused. You mock the service-layer collaborators with `@MockBean` so the controller is tested in isolation, then you use `WebTestClient` to send a request and make fluent assertions: `webTestClient.post().uri("/api/v1/transfers").bodyValue(request).exchange().expectStatus().isCreated().expectBody().jsonPath("$.status").isEqualTo("COMPLETED")`. This verifies routing, request deserialization, bean validation, status codes, and response serialization — everything about how others talk to you.

The two are not competitors; they test different seams and are often used together. A realistic slice test of the payments controller uses `WebTestClient` to drive the endpoint and `@MockBean` to stub the service. A realistic test of the credit-score client uses `MockWebServer` to stand in for the bureau. The senior nuances: `WebTestClient` can also bind to a running server for full end-to-end tests, but its most valuable use is the sliced `@WebFluxTest`; `MockWebServer` requires you to remember to shut the server down in teardown and to assert the recorded request, otherwise you only tested that a response came back, not that you sent the right one; and for a test that spans your controller all the way to a real downstream, you can combine both — `WebTestClient` at the front door and `MockWebServer` at the back. Choosing the wrong tool is a classic mistake: trying to test outbound resilience with `WebTestClient` tests nothing about your client, and trying to test your controller with `MockWebServer` tests nothing about your routing.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh builds a loan-eligibility service. It has an inbound REST endpoint that customers call, and it makes an outbound call to an external credit-bureau API. Both seams need tests, and they need different tools.

Problem 1 — The service calls the credit bureau over HTTP. In production the bureau sometimes returns a 500, sometimes a 404 for an unknown customer, and sometimes responds slowly. Rajesh's client must retry on 500, map 404 to a clean domain exception, and time out on slow responses. He cannot test this against the real bureau — it is flaky, rate-limited, and costs money per call. This is exactly what MockWebServer solves: a real local server that pretends to be the bureau and can be scripted to return 500, 404, or a slow response so the client's resilience is proven.

Problem 2 — The service exposes `POST /api/v1/eligibility`. It must reject requests with a missing account ID with 400, return 200 with an eligibility decision for valid requests, and never leak internal errors. Rajesh needs to test the controller's routing, validation, and response shaping without starting the whole application or calling the real bureau. This is exactly what WebTestClient with @WebFluxTest and @MockBean solves: drive the endpoint in-memory with the service mocked.

The mini-project builds both seams. We write `CreditBureauClient` (uses WebClient, the outbound seam) and `EligibilityController` plus `EligibilityService` (the inbound seam). Then we write the two kinds of tests side by side so the decision is concrete: a MockWebServer test proving retry and error mapping on the client, and a WebTestClient test proving validation and status codes on the controller.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two test scenarios — an outbound call to the credit bureau, and an inbound call to our own eligibility endpoint.

Step 1 (MockWebServer, outbound): The test starts a real `MockWebServer` on a random local port and enqueues a 500 followed by a 200 returning the score 760. It builds a `CreditBureauClient` pointed at the server's URL.

Step 2: The test calls `fetchScore("SAV2001")`. The client really sends a GET over loopback. The server replies 500, so the client's retry logic sends the request again, and the server replies 200 with 760. `StepVerifier` asserts the stream emits 760 and completes.

Step 3: The test pulls the `RecordedRequest` and asserts the method was GET and the path was `/scores/SAV2001`. This proves the client built the correct outbound request — the thing only MockWebServer can verify. The 404 and slow-response tests similarly prove error mapping and timeout.

Step 4: In teardown the server is shut down so the port is released.

Step 5 (WebTestClient, inbound): A separate `@WebFluxTest` loads only the controller. The `EligibilityService` is a `@MockBean`, so no real bureau is touched. `WebTestClient` posts a valid body; the controller deserializes it, validation passes, the mocked service returns an APPROVED decision, and the test asserts status 200 and the JSON fields.

Step 6: `WebTestClient` posts a body with no account ID. Bean validation fails before any service call, and the controller returns 400. This proves our routing and validation — the thing only WebTestClient tests.

Final output:

```text
CreditBureauClientTest
 retriesOnServerErrorThenSucceeds   (GET /scores/SAV2001, 500 then 200 → 760)
 mapsNotFoundToDomainException      (404 → BureauUnavailableException)
 timesOutOnSlowBureau               (5s body delay > 2s timeout → exception)
EligibilityControllerTest
 validRequestReturns200WithDecision (200, status=APPROVED, score=760)
 missingAccountIdReturns400         (validation → 400, no downstream call)
BUILD SUCCESS — 5 tests, 0 failures
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
OkHttp MockWebServer and Spring's WebTestClient solve opposite problems, and I choose between them by looking at the direction of the call under test. If I am testing code that calls out to another service — a WebClient or RestClient fetching a credit score or posting to a payment gateway — then the thing I need to fake is the downstream server, and that is MockWebServer. If I am testing my own controller, the code that receives requests, then I need a client that drives my endpoints, and that is WebTestClient. The one-line rule I keep in my head is that MockWebServer tests the calls my service makes outward, and WebTestClient tests the calls others make inward.

MockWebServer is a real, lightweight HTTP server that binds to a local port. I enqueue scripted responses, point my client at its URL, run my code, and then I do two things that matter. I assert the actual request my code sent — the method, path, query, headers, and body — by reading the recorded request, because that is where outbound bugs usually hide. And I simulate downstream failure: I enqueue a 500 to prove my retry logic retries, a 404 to prove I map it to a clean domain exception, and a delayed response to prove my timeout fires. Because it is a real server speaking real HTTP, it exercises my whole client stack rather than a mock of it, which is exactly what I want when testing resilience.

WebTestClient goes the other way. With the WebFluxTest slice, Spring loads only my web layer, not the whole application, so the test is fast and focused, and I mock the service-layer collaborators so the controller is tested in isolation. Then WebTestClient sends requests to my endpoint and I make fluent assertions about status codes, JSON fields, and validation behavior. That verifies routing, request deserialization, bean validation, and response serialization — everything about how others talk to me. The classic mistake is swapping them: trying to test outbound resilience with WebTestClient tells me nothing about my client, and trying to test my controller's routing with MockWebServer tells me nothing about my endpoints.

At the National Bank of India I used both on our loan-eligibility service, and they were complementary rather than competing. The service calls an external credit bureau, which in production is flaky, rate-limited, and costs money per call, so I could not test against it directly. I used MockWebServer to stand in for the bureau and scripted it to return a 500 so I could prove the client retried, a 404 so I could prove it mapped to our BureauUnavailableException, and a slow response so I could prove the two-second timeout fired. Separately, the service exposes a POST eligibility endpoint, and I used WebTestClient with the WebFluxTest slice and a mocked service to prove that a missing account ID returns 400 and a valid request returns 200 with the right decision, all in memory with no bureau involved. For a full end-to-end slice I even combined them — WebTestClient at the front door and MockWebServer at the back — but the key judgment the interviewer is looking for is that the direction of the call decides the tool.
